input: In the process under consideration, liquid-liquid extraction is employed to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream by transferring it into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of the acetic acid, defined as the ratio of its concentration in the organic phase to its concentration in the aqueous phase, is 1.71 at 25 °C, and the design is based on 4 countercurrent stages. On this basis, the predicted recovery is 95% of the acetic acid present in the feed. Because the distribution coefficient is greater than unity, the solvent is favoured as the receiving phase, and the countercurrent arrangement ensures that the freshest solvent comes into contact with the most thoroughly depleted raffinate, so that a useful driving force is maintained throughout the cascade rather than being exhausted at the feed end. Each successive stage recovers a further portion of the acid remaining in the aqueous phase, and the combined effect of the stages is to reduce the acid content of the raffinate to the stated residual fraction. The prediction is, however, subject to two significant assumptions. In the first place, the stages are assumed to be equilibrium stages, meaning that the two phases leaving any stage are taken to be in full equilibrium with one another at the stated distribution coefficient. In the second place, mutual solubility between the phases is assumed to be negligible, so that the flow rate of each phase can be treated as constant from stage to stage. Neither of these assumptions has yet been verified for the actual solvents concerned. If the stage efficiency falls short of the equilibrium ideal, or if appreciable mutual solubility occurs, the recovery actually achieved would be expected to fall below 95%, and experimental confirmation on the real solvent system would be required before the figure could be relied upon.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous feed into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of acetic acid, taken as the concentration in the organic phase over the concentration in the aqueous phase, is 1.71 at 25 °C. The design uses 4 countercurrent stages. The predicted recovery is 95% of the acetic acid in the feed. A distribution coefficient above unity favours the solvent, and countercurrent contact lets the leanest solvent meet the most depleted raffinate, so the driving force is held along the whole cascade rather than spent at the feed end. Each added stage recovers part of what the earlier stages left, and the stages together bring the raffinate down to the stated fraction of the feed content. The extract leaves loaded with the recovered acid, and the raffinate leaves carrying the fraction the cascade did not take. The solvent rate is the remaining design handle, and it is set high enough that the aqueous phase is nowhere close to saturation against the solvent it meets at any stage, which keeps the stated coefficient in force along the whole cascade rather than only at the feed end where the concentrations are highest. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages: the two phases leaving each stage are taken to be in equilibrium with each other, at the distribution coefficient stated. The prediction also assumes negligible mutual solubility, so the flow of each phase is treated as unchanged from stage to stage and the solvent is treated as free of feed components other than the transferred acid. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. Stage efficiency below the equilibrium value would lower the recovery at the stated stage count, and mutual solubility would change both phase flows and the effective distribution. The 95% is therefore the recovery of the ideal cascade on the actual feed only if the two assumptions hold closely enough on the solvents in use; a test on the actual solvents settles both points and has not been reported.
